projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Lincoln N. Christensen was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Lincoln N. Christensen. Mr. Christensen served in the US Army with the 403rd AAA battalion. He served in North Africa, Sicily and Italy, and his highest rank was first lieutenant. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Christensen's home in Mentor, Ohio on March 11th, of 2003. Lincoln was 84 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: On East 90th Street near Euclid Avenue in Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you then?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I was 19 years old.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of Pearl Harbor, the Pearl Harbor attack?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I was in a movie in Biloxi, Mississippi when they interrupted the movie and announced the Pearl Harbor attack and that every military -- all military personnel was to return to camp, which we all did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So obviously you were already in the Army at that point. When did you join the Army?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: September 1940.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Enlisted, I assume, right, at that point? Was there a draft in 1940?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: It had just started. I was early.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: And I was drafted into the infantry and sent to Columbus, Ohio, and while there it was suggested that anyone who desired to join the air corps could take a departure from the infantry and join the air corps, and that would be a second enlistment, so one would go from a salary of 21 dollars a month to 36 dollars a month. Quite a few people took that; I was one. And I was sent to Biloxi, Mississippi, which was a large air corps establishment where they had fish for breakfast. They had me lined up to become an aircraft mechanic, and the Army or the air corps had no idea how terrible a mechanic I would have been. Instead they asked for volunteers to cadre a new airfield in Sebring, Florida, and they needed personnel with some banking experience or accounting education or whatever, so I volunteered for that and was moved to Sebring, Florida; lived in a hotel for a few weeks and then moved out to the camp and was put in the officers' page section and went from private and in three months was a sec sergeant. That's how empty the field was when we got there. The major in charge suggested that another guy and myself put in for officers training school at Duke University, and we did; however, the Army was sorely in need of officers, evidently, in the antiaircraft part, and Lee and I were sent to Camp Davis to become officers in the antiaircraft, and this was a mistake on the part of the Army for sure. I know they could have found someone more qualified -- I lose my teeth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Well, in any event, I graduated from there and was on overseas orders from Norfolk, Virginia and landed in North Africa and joined the battalion, antiaircraft battalion there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: About when would that have been?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I couldn't tell you. It was in the summer of '42.

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you joined the antiaircraft battalion there?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: And the war was pretty much over in North Africa. We didn't see any action there, but we were in the invasion of Sicily and Italy as an antiaircraft unit, 90 millimeter.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How early did you go in on the Sicily invasion?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: We were on the initial invasion.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The first wave or early waves?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So with the antiaircraft people, would you hit the beach then with the rest of them?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes, we hit the beach and were set up to protect the beach from German aircraft.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What are your specific memories of that day?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: The best memory I have was that the men who operated the LST had fresh eggs for breakfast. Other than that, it was wet and hot and dry, and there was no action at all. The Germans didn't bother much with airplanes. There were a lot of our airplanes but very -- I doubt if there were any at all of theirs. I didn't see any.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you see any combat when you were still in Africa?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So was your first combat activity there in Sicily then?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: The invasion of Sicily.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day when you were actually facing the enemy?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Well, we didn't face the enemy because we were antiaircraft and we were 90 millimeters, which is a large gun in antiaircraft, or was, and the enemy was long gone by the time we got there. We were primarily set up to -- for the safety of landing troops and supporting groups on the invasion. I would guess they had probably chased the Germans about halfway up the island by the time we got there. By the time we got up to Northern Sicily, the invasion of Italy was pretty much ready to go.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other memories of anything unusual happening on Sicily?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Well, the most unusual thing there was we were set up outside, made a ring around the seashore villa where George Patton was living at the time. There wasn't much going on. The German air corps was pretty much decimated by the time we got there. The smaller 40 millimeter guns had more contact with the enemy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever get close to General Patton?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I was fined 50 dollars by General Patton for not having a helmet on my head in North Africa. It was so hot that I had taken the helmet and helmet liner off and was sitting in a Jeep directing our battalion vehicles, and he came along with his entourage and noticed that I didn't have my helmet on and fined me 50 dollars on the spot. I got no receipt for it. So that was my contact with him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, that would have been about a month's pay or more, right?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, boy. So anything else from Sicily that you remember?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: No. It was a good time in Sicily because there was no action there; it was just like going camping. We were fed three meals a day and had plenty of rest, no action. Evidently the Germans didn't care whether General Patton made it or not at that time, but really the German air corps was pretty decimated. They couldn't do much. The last thing I heard of them was when they bombed Naples Harbor. Well, we sat up north of Naples.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So where did you invade Italy?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I don't remember the dates.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The dates are okay, but was it Salerno, is that where you landed, or was it somewhere else?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes, we went across at Salerno, all the troops did, because it was such a narrow strait there, and they had already run the Germans up past Naples, so our battalion went up and set up around Naples in the airfield that was close by, and that was used by aircraft to bring in fresh food for Fifth Army headquarters, and I know that because I was -- I spent two weeks on detached service at Fifth Army headquarters and dined with the officers there on fresh meat, mashed potatoes, fresh vegetables. It was like a vacation. Well, the war went so fast up to the Cassino area that we just stayed north of Naples until the Army stopped at the Rapido River. Then we were sent up to guard the bridges across the Rapido River. At that point our mission was changed from antiaircraft to field artillery, and that winter was a miserable time; not the most miserable, but very miserable.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything special to try to keep warm that winter?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Oh, yes. We dug in the ground and set up sand bags around. And when it rained, the rain would seep into the ground into the worm holes and then into the area that we were using during the night for sleeping and dampen everything, if not thoroughly wetting it. My most -- the worst experience, though, was, since we were changed to artillery, we had an observation post on the top of a hill overlooking the river and looking at the Cassino area, and they sent me up there to be a forward observer, and a forward observer would be the one who selected targets, gave the coordinates to the battery or the battalion, and then they would fire and you would observe to see how close they were and give any corrections needed, and I had no idea in the world what was going on with that. I had no prior experience or prior education in field artillery, and how I got up there I don't know. But it seems like the Army, when it needs a body, furnishes the body for whatever. I had a friend who was of German extraction and studied German in college as his first choice. He was sent to the South Pacific as a medic assistant. Oh, well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As a forward observer, you could read a map and try to give them coordinates to show, right?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Well, yes, but at the time you were doing this the Germans knew that there were like five or six of us up there on that little ridge, and they kept sending shells our way. And although we were behind them and the shells couldn't reach us, it was disconcerting to hear that noise all day long. I was glad when they left Cassino. Well, they finally did. We were able to watch the bombing of the monastery. You --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, how long -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: You have to realize, it's been a long time since I've even talked about this. Well, at any rate, by the time we picked up and left those positions around the bridge, we moved up to the mountains just before the Po Valley and spent another winter up there. That was pretty miserable too. Winter in the mountains isn't very much fun if you're living in a tent or a hole in the ground.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes, had close buddies among the officers and the enlisted men. One guy I think of fondly often is a fellow named Howenstein who was our mail man. He went to battalion headquarters every day to pick up the mail. He was 45 or 46 years old at the time. I was in my early 20s and suffering, and here this guy was enjoying himself. He thought this was great. Well, that position we had we were shelled several times by the German artillery. That was pretty scary -- very scary. And then finally they cleaned out the Po Valley and we moved up north of Florence, and I got to make several trips into Florence, which I enjoyed immensely. And then the battalion took over a German prisoner camp and repatriated the Germans to a small town in Austria, and there were thousands of men. We would send the men on a flatbed 18-wheeled truck, jammed tight with standing prisoners, up to this little town; took one day, one full day, to make the trip.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So where were you on VE Day then when the war in Europe ended?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: We were in the mountains before the Po Valley.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything to celebrate on that day?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: We didn't know it was VE Day; at our level we didn't. They might have known it at Fifth Army headquarters -- they should have known it. We found out the next day. Everyone was quite happy and we had a lot of Italian wine to toast.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get along okay with the Italian people when you were in that camp?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Oh, yes. I always admired the Italians. Wherever we went we would find some women who would be willing to do our laundry, and when you first get there, you would say how much, and they would say, oh, 25 Lira. After we'd been there a few days, they did more laundry, you'd say how much, they'd say, whatever you think it's worth. You would never give them 25 Lira, you'd give them 200 or 500; so they learned, or I learned how smart they were. There were many other ways that you learned that too, which I wouldn't want to say here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Maybe this is a related topic. Did you guys get much of a break from combat? Did you have any entertainment?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: No, we never had entertainment. We had General Eisenhower come to our position for lunch one day while we were at Cassino, and the photographer took his picture as he stood in line with his mess kit; and after that was done, after the photographing was done, he then went to a tent that we had erected with a table and chairs, and the Fifth Army catering service brought in the meal. So although he had photographs of being in line, he sure didn't eat the same food that the guys in line ate. Well, he was a three-star general. What do you expect?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you didn't get any closer to him? You didn't get in any trouble with General Eisenhower, did you?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: What about the white glove?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: That was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Inspection?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: No, that was during the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: After the war ended and we got these troops into Austria, the battalion was to go to the Pacific, and I had a friend who was a friend of a friend at Fifth Army headquarters, and I got transferred to the military police of Fifth Army headquarters. There was a height restriction. You couldn't be any shorter than 6 feet, 2 inches, and you had to have a straight military bearing, and I passed because I was 6'5" and stood pretty straight. I spent the remainder of my overseas career at that Lake Garda Italy, Northern Italy. That was quite enjoyable. One thing I would have to say, all the time overseas as an officer while in the artillery I was issued a carbine and never fired it. I kept it clean, but I never fired it. And when I transferred to the MPs, I was issued a 45 and fired that once on a railroad embankment at a bunch of cans. If I had had to shoot it in earnest at some people, for whatever reason, I doubt that I would have made that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you become an officer?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: That was late '41. I've got pictures of it but...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was your highest rank then during World War II?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Made first lieutenant finally. The headquarters of Fifth Army put out a bulletin stating that any officer who had been overseas three months as a second lieutenant would automatically become a first lieutenant, and much against the wishes of our battalion commander, two other officers and myself became first lieutenants.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why was he against that?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: He thought it was too rapid a promotion. He was a lieutenant colonel, and he was in the same graduating class as Mark Clark, who was a three-star general, and I was sure he had feelings about that, whatever it took for him to get promotion was -- whoever promoted people like that didn't see it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters, packages from home?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Oh, yes, I got two letters a week from my mother, and I had a girlfriend, got a letter from her about once a week or every other week, got packages from my mother. Didn't hear much from anybody else; didn't write to anybody else.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would you write when you did write?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Mostly about the weather and being in a dugout hole and have the water come down the worm tracks in the hole and flood us out. I was the censor of the mail, and I felt I couldn't say a whole lot because I had to keep others from saying a whole lot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would you have to cut out of their mail?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Strangely enough, I never cut anything out or never inked over. In my view none of the men ever said anything or wrote anything that I felt needed to be censored. I mean, you could say you're on a mountain in Italy, and who, you know, who are you going to give out information about that. And we didn't know enough about the strategy of the war to give anything away. {Laughing.}

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did something come to mind there?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes. Actually, I guess this happens to most people: I remember the good times, or what I call good times, more than I do the bad things. Like I remember in North Africa going to a dance put on by the nurses of the hospital, and I remember being in Sicily and taking a trip, sight-seeing trip, through Palermo. I remember a restaurant high up on the hill in Naples that at night, while eating dinner, you could look over the whole valley with the city and the musicians that played music while you were eating. I remember trips through Florence. I remember going through the Brenner pass up through the Alps. I remember the times as military police in Fifth Army headquarters, Northern Italy. Seems like all I remember's the good times. Have to look at the photographs to see the bad times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, when you -- were you part of the convoy that escorted those prisoners up to Austria then?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your group was part of that?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Well, they sent one every day, and we would go up one day, stay overnight, drive back the next day and then have a day off. They had four of us doing that. The Russians that we had in the camp were mainly -- I don't know what you'd call them. They had an oriental feature to their face, and we were told by the residents of the Austrian village that if the Russian soldier didn't have identification papers, they were machine-gunned and thrown into a common grave, and according to the local people there were hundreds and hundreds of them. And the reason they did that was because they didn't have the railroad facilities to haul them back to Russia, so the only ones who could get back were ones who were able to present papers showing who they were and where they had been, and I could see how easily they could lose those.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when was that taking place that they were doing that? Was that after the war?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: After the war, sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And it was the Austrian people that were doing this?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Oh, no, it was the Russians who were doing it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The Russians were doing it to their own?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Oh, yes, but they didn't feel as though they were their own because they were -- the men who were in the German Army at the end of the war were primarily made of Russian soldiers, and these were Russians from Northern Russia, and I don't remember what they called them, but they were -- they were looked down upon. They were highly uneducated. You walked through the streets of this little town, and the people would say, when are you -- when are you coming, when are the United States Army -- when is it coming? Because they were under Russian rule at that time, and the Russians that were in that area were very, very bad, they were bad news. They were -- they would go up to a house, maybe six, maybe 12 would go up to a house and say they're going to stay there. They would make the people feed them. They would not use the toilet facilities, either in the house or outdoors. Luckily we didn't see any of that because we were there such a short time and it was nighttime, and we were quartered in a small hotel, myself and the drivers. And the Russian officers would not permit us to wander the streets, so we didn't have that much contact with the local residents, just mostly the hotel people. And it was a beautiful town.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the name of that town?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But it was a town in Austria somewhere?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes. It was just over the border from Northern Italy. And I guess the Russians had Austria among all the contra'd areas that they had. We had no contact with anybody up there. We had no contact with the Russians at all, just two or three officers who told us where to go and where we would be housed that night and the strict rules about going out into the town.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many of those trips did you make then?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I made three. Others made more. I only made three because I transferred away to the Fifth Army headquarters.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the name of you're outfit before that, the artillery outfit?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: That was the 403 AAA battalion.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you attached to the Fifth Army the whole time?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: We were attached to the second corps which was part of the Fifth Army. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: If I had stayed in the battalion, I would have been home quite early because the war ended before they could get shipped out to the Asian theater, so they came directly home. I had to stay in the Fifth Army headquarters until they shut that down, and that was -- I'm probably way off -- that was in the spring of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '46 maybe?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: '46, yes, somewhere in there. Because I came back to get discharged at Camp, whatever, in Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What would that be? I can't remember. I've heard it a million times, but I can't remember it right now. I think I know what town you're talking about in Pennsylvania though. Indian Town Gap?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Indian Town Gap.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Well, my mother was happy to see me. My brother was an officer in the -- medical officer in the South Pacific, and he was still there. That was the only family we had; branched out since then.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Tell him about the white glove.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think that's coming up if we talk a little bit about the Korean thing. We're almost out of tape here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience during World War II, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: I don't think about it. I don't think about -- as I told you, the photograph album, that's been 25 years or more since I've had that out and looked at it. I view it as just some part of my life that, just like working and raising a family, it's there to think about if something jars you, you know. I wouldn't be talking about it now if it weren't for you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Not buddies, but we did lose men in the battalion. Early on I found out it wasn't good to establish a close relationship because one kept moving and -- from here to there, and you really -- really had no idea what was going to happen. Had one close friend, when I was in Florida, by the name of Lee Harris who was from Meridian, Mississippi, and he and I became very close. We did a lot of weekend traveling in Florida, and I enjoyed his company; but then when we went to OCS, he was in a different unit. He went one way and I went another, and this is true all through Army life.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it was pretty rare to have a buddy you had in basic training right on through?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Oh, sure. I guess the Army made an attempt at keeping buddies together because of lack of enlistment, but when the Army was full of people, they just moved bodies around. That's the way I feel about the Army was they were body movers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you stayed in the reserves and then almost went to Korea, right?

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Yes. I signed up for the reserves, got married, had two children, and the Korean War bloomed, and I was recalled for that. I was sent to Camp Breckenridge in Kentucky, and my wife and children finally came down and lived, not in Evansville but whatever town that is across the river from Evansville.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Henderson.

sp.speaker: Lincoln N. Christensen
sp.p: Henderson, Kentucky. That was quite an experience there. I got into trouble one day because I took the battery out to the rifle range for rifle training on the coldest, wintriest, rainiest, snowiest, windiest day of the year. The targets kept blowing off whatever they were hooked on, and the men would fire their rifle and it would freeze in the open position. Finally I called battalion headquarters and recommended that we leave there and go to someplace where we could have lectures or whatever; and I was told, when you're in Korea fighting, you don't stop fighting because of the weather, you keep going. So we stayed out there, and I didn't think that was a good idea, sending these young kids overseas when they got through their eight weeks training with that kind of a background. And the biggest trouble I ran into was during an inspection by the general in charge of the camp he came and inspected Battery A, which was run by a captain who had returned from Korea, and the captain had closed off all the coal fired barrel furnaces in the barracks and white washed the insides and had done similar things with the rest of the insides of the barracks, and he was highly thought of by the general. When the general came to B Battery, I had left the coal fires going all night, and they were still on fire in the middle of the morning, and the general came in with his entourage, and he saw those -- I forget what -- they're cast iron stoves. Each floor of the barracks had three of them, and they burned dirty Kentucky coal. Anyway, he came in, stopped in front of that first stove, reached out his hand toward his aide who put a white glove in his hand, and the aide opened the door to the stove, and the general ran his hand across the door of the stove and came up with a hand full of soot, which he showed to me. And it wasn't too long before I was on orders for Korea because I had failed the inspection. Well, I was in California waiting orders to board a boat or plane when my mother, who had been doing some behind-the-scenes work, got a good friend of hers who was a congressional representative to have me removed from the orders to go overseas and return to Indian Town Gap again in Pennsylvania, and I lasted out the rest of my career in the Army there. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's about it?
